summary: Evolution vocabulary for ages 10–11: binding ~9 terms (adaptation, evolution, natural selection, extinct/extinction, fossil record, species, common ancestor, variation, and lightly mutation) to concrete examples, AND assembling the mechanism words into the natural-selection sequence in the correct order. Two distinctions are high-value: extinct vs endangered, and adaptation (the feature/outcome) vs natural selection (the process). Learners first fix each word's meaning against a vivid example, then order the words into the story of natural selection; usage is exercised in live narrative, not just recognition.
misconceptions: Confusing extinct and endangered (using 'extinct' for at-risk species that still survive).
Conflating adaptation (a feature/outcome) with natural selection (the process that produces it), or using 'evolution' and 'adaptation' interchangeably.
Using the mechanism words out of order or dropping steps (e.g. 'natural selection' without variation or a selection pressure).
Teleology — 'evolution tries to make animals better / has a goal' embedded in how the words are used.
Lamarckian phrasing sneaking back in ('the species adapted itself because it needed to').
Treating 'mutation' as always harmful or as a conscious change, rather than a random source of new variation.
Thinking 'common ancestor' means one species descended directly from a living one (e.g. 'humans came from monkeys').

activities.title: Evolution glossary gallery: term pinned to an example
steps: Explore a rich scene where each key term lives on something concrete the learner can point to and reveal: a camel reveals 'adaptation — a feature that helps it survive here'; a dodo reveals 'extinct — none left anywhere'; layered rock reveals 'fossil record — the trail of evidence in the rocks'; a point where two branches meet reveals 'common ancestor — the shared origin'.
Read each term used in a real sentence at the moment of reveal, so meaning and usage arrive together rather than as a recited definition.
Use a lift-the-flap / contrast pair that sets the extinct dodo directly beside a tiger labelled 'endangered — still here, but at risk', and say aloud why each word fits its creature.
At the common-ancestor branch point, explain why it does NOT mean one living species descended directly from another (e.g. heading off 'humans came from monkeys').
After exploring, say each term in a fresh sentence of the learner's own to confirm usage, not just recognition.
activities.insight: Each technical term names something specific and concrete; the exact line between extinct (gone forever) and endangered (few left, still surviving) and between adaptation (the feature an organism has) and the across-generations process that produces it matters.

activities.title: Assemble the natural-selection mechanism in order
steps: Build the mechanism as an ordered chain, placing the steps in the correct sequence: inherited variation exists within the population → a selection pressure acts in the environment → better-suited individuals survive and reproduce more, passing on their helpful features → over many generations the population changes (evolution).
If a step is placed out of order (e.g. selection or reproduction before any variation exists), fix it and say why variation must come first.
Ideally label the stages of a selection animation or story the learner has already seen work — dropping the right term onto each stage — so the words attach to a process they have already observed.
State in the learner's own words what 'variation', 'selection pressure', and 'reproduction' each contribute to the chain.
Say where 'mutation' fits: a new change in inherited information that can add fresh variation — kept light, with no molecular/DNA detail.
activities.insight: 'Natural selection' is not a single label but an ordered chain: variation must already exist before a selection pressure can act on it, and the population change (evolution) emerges over many generations. Evolution is the outcome/change over time; natural selection is the mechanism that drives it.

activities.title: Tell the moth story using the words in sequence (use-in-context)
steps: Tell the story of how a population of moths in a sooty, polluted city came to be mostly dark-coloured, using these words in a sensible order as you go: variation, adaptation, natural selection, reproduction.

Explain why 'extinct' would NOT be the right word if pale moths became very rare in the city: pale and dark moths are colour forms of the same species, and extinction means a whole species (every member, everywhere) has died out. Then say how 'extinct' differs from 'endangered', using real species as examples.

Answer probing follow-ups in your own words: what exactly was the selection pressure in the moth story? Could a single moth 'evolve' in its lifetime, or does that word apply to the population over generations — and which word goes with which? Give a real animal that is extinct and one that is endangered, saying why each word fits. Where does 'mutation' fit as a source of new variation?
activities.insight: Genuine command shows in sequenced USE within a live narrative — using each term precisely and in order, and cleanly distinguishing extinct from endangered with examples — not in reciting isolated definitions.

checkQuestion: Tell the story of how a population of moths in a sooty, polluted city came to be mostly dark-coloured, using these words in a sensible order as you go: variation, adaptation, natural selection, reproduction. Then tell me what 'extinct' would mean for the pale moths, and how that's different from 'endangered'.
checkAnswer: The child uses the terms in a correct sequence: there was variation (pale and dark moths); dark colour was an adaptation suiting the sooty trees; birds ate the more visible pale moths (a selection pressure), so dark moths survived and passed on their colour through reproduction (natural selection); if every last pale moth died out they would be extinct, whereas endangered means very few remain but some still survive.
